title: Baking soda meets vinegar
interaction: A beaker of vinegar particles. One control: how many spoonfuls of baking soda to tip in. Each baking-soda particle that meets a vinegar particle turns into a bubble of gas that rises out of the beaker, and a counter tallies the bubbles. Tip in more soda than there is vinegar and the fizzing stops with white powder left on the bottom; pour in more vinegar instead and the powder all goes. A second run puts the gas to work: the same fizz inflates a balloon over the bottle neck, or lifts a muffin batter in a warm oven, where baking powder is baking soda sold with its own dry acid.
takeaway: The fizz is a new substance, a gas, made one particle from one particle, so it stops the moment either ingredient runs out, and the leftovers can never be turned back into vinegar and powder.
needsSource: none
pitfall: The bubbles are not air that was hiding in the powder, and the fizzing does not go on for ever: the amount of gas is fixed by whichever ingredient runs out first.

title: Bubbles and foam
interaction: A wand and a dish of liquid. Dip and blow: with plain water the film snaps back before it can close; with soapy water a film stretches, pinches off and pulls itself round. The film is a mesh of points pulled by surface tension that the reader can poke and watch spring back into a sphere; press two bubbles together and a flat wall forms between them; swap in a square wand and the bubble still comes out round. Last, whip the soapy water into a foam and scrub time to watch the walls drain thin and the bubbles pop from the top down.
takeaway: A bubble is a skin of water that soap lets stretch, and the skin pulls itself into the shape with the least surface for the air inside, a sphere, whatever the wand's shape.
needsSource: none; a surface-tension spring-mesh film model
pitfall: Soap does not make the film stronger; it makes it stretchier and slower to drain. And a bubble is not round because of the wand or because air 'pushes equally': the film shrinks to the smallest surface it can.

title: Why wet things dry

needsSource: IUPAC/CIAAW isotopic abundances (freely available); MassBank of North America spectra (CC BY 4.0) for comparison.

title: NMR: spins, pulses & spectra
interaction: Put nuclear spins in a magnetic field, fire a 90° pulse and watch the net magnetization tip and precess while the detector records the decaying signal, then Fourier-transform it into a peak. Add a second spin with a scalar coupling and the peak splits into a doublet; set real chemical shifts for ethanol's three environments and watch the whole spectrum assemble, with linewidth following the decay rate.
takeaway: An NMR spectrometer listens to nuclei precessing after a pulse, and each nucleus's note is shifted by its electron surroundings and split by its neighbours, so the spectrum reads out the molecule's structure.
needs: Chemical shifts and coupling constants for a few molecules (ethanol, ethyl acetate).
pitfall: The spectrum is not scanned one frequency at a time; it is the Fourier transform of one decaying signal, and 'spin' does not mean the nucleus is physically spinning like a top.
why: OCR A-level Chemistry A (H432) module 6 includes proton and carbon-13 NMR with a chemical-shift data sheet: https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/exam-specifications/a-level/chemistry/ocr/
overlapWith: medical-imaging: that page closes with MRI in a sentence; this one simulates the spin physics behind the signal and reads chemistry from it.
needsSource: nmrshiftdb2 (University of Cologne), published under an open-content licence as stated on its site (no named CC licence; confirm), or literature shift values.

title: Nucleation & crystal growth
interaction: Cool a simulated liquid below its freezing point and watch small clusters form and dissolve until one passes the critical size and grows, while a plot of the free energy of a cluster against its radius shows the hill it had to climb; deepen the undercooling and the hill shrinks, more nuclei survive and the solid ends up as many small grains instead of a few large ones. Then run a phase-field model of a solidifying front on a grid and watch it break into dendrites whose arms thin as the undercooling rises.
takeaway: A liquid below its freezing point does not freeze at once: a solid seed must first grow past a critical size against its own surface, so deeper undercooling means more seeds and finer grains, and a growing front splits into branches.
pitfall: Freezing does not start everywhere at once when the freezing point is reached; pure water can be cooled well below 0 °C, and snowflakes branch because the front is unstable, not because the molecules know a shape.
why: MIT OCW 3.205's calendar runs from diffusion to nucleation, solidification, spinodal decomposition and coarsening: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-205-thermodynamics-and-kinetics-of-materials-fall-2006/pages/calendar
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page freezes a box at the freezing point; this one shows why it needs a seed, how far it can be undercooled and what shape the solid takes.
needsSource: none

title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence & photochemistry
interaction: Shine a light pulse on a population of molecules shown on a Jablonski ladder and watch them climb and then leave the excited state by competing routes (fluorescence, internal conversion, intersystem crossing, phosphorescence), each with a rate constant on a slider. A plot of emitted light against time shows the lifetime and quantum yield; switch the lamp off to see the slow phosphorescent tail, and add a quencher to watch the Stern-Volmer line steepen.
takeaway: After absorbing a photon a molecule has several exits with different speeds, and how bright and how long it glows is decided by that race.
needs: Rate constants, lifetimes and quantum yields for a couple of real fluorophores.
pitfall: Fluorescence is not reflection and not stored light: the emitted photon carries less energy than the absorbed one because some was lost as heat first (the Stokes shift).
why: MIT OCW 5.61's syllabus ends with molecular spectroscopy and photochemistry: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/chemistry/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/index.htm
overlapWith: vision-color: that page mixes light in the eye; this one models what one molecule does with a photon after absorbing it.
needsSource: Published lifetimes and quantum yields (e.g. fluorescein, anthracene) from the literature; numbers only, no licensed dataset.

title: Quantum dots: color from size
interaction: Slide the radius of a semiconductor nanocrystal from 2 to 10 nm and the page solves the confinement energy of its electron and hole, adds the bulk band gap and shows the color it emits, next to a ladder of discrete levels that spreads as the dot shrinks. Switch the material and compare the computed emission with measured peak wavelengths of real dots; a density-of-states panel shows the smooth bulk band breaking into sharp levels as the box closes in.
takeaway: Trap an electron in a box a few nanometres wide and the energy it gives back as light is set by the size of the box, so one material glows in every color depending on how small it is made.
needs: Effective masses, bulk gaps and dielectric constants for CdSe, CdS and InP, and measured size-to-emission data.
pitfall: The color is not a different chemical or a dye inside the dot: it is the confinement energy added to the same material's gap, and bigger dots are redder, not bluer.
why: The 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots: https://www.bu.edu/nano-bu/?p=5287
overlapWith: solar-cells: that page uses a bulk band gap; this one shows the gap itself depending on size once the crystal is nanometres wide.
needsSource: Material parameters from the literature; size-to-wavelength calibration from Yu, Qu, Guo & Peng, Chem. Mater. 2003 (published numbers, no licensed dataset).

title: Free energy & the equilibrium constant
interaction: Drag the extent of a reaction (N2O4 ⇌ 2 NO2, with real enthalpy and entropy) along a plot of the mixture's Gibbs energy and watch it fall to a minimum part-way, where the composition matches the equilibrium constant; switch off the mixing-entropy term that bends the curve to see why the reaction would otherwise run to completion. Change the temperature and the pressure and watch the minimum, K and the yield move.
takeaway: A reaction runs downhill in free energy and stops at the bottom of a curve that lies at a mixture rather than at completion, because mixing itself lowers the free energy; the depth of that bottom is the equilibrium constant.
needs: Standard enthalpies of formation and entropies for N2O4 and NO2.
pitfall: A negative ΔG° does not mean the reaction goes to completion and a positive one does not mean it does not happen; the sign sets K, and the mixture always settles at a minimum between the two extremes.
why: MIT OCW 5.60 Thermodynamics & Kinetics covers chemical equilibrium of gas- and solution-phase reactions through the Gibbs energy: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008
overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page reaches equilibrium kinetically, as equal forward and reverse rates; this one locates it thermodynamically as the minimum of G and ties it to K and temperature.
needsSource: NIST-JANAF thermochemical tables (NIST Standard Reference Data, free to use with citation; a few numbers).

title: Rubber & polymer chains: the entropic spring
interaction: Grab the ends of a freely-jointed chain of a few hundred links and pull; the page samples the chain's random walks and shows the count of shapes that fit each end-to-end distance collapsing, with the restoring force computed from that count and the temperature. Turn up the temperature and the stretched chain pulls harder and shortens; cross-link many chains into a network and rubber's stress-strain curve appears beside Hooke's law, with the warming on stretching shown on a thermometer.
takeaway: Rubber pulls back not because its bonds are stretched but because a stretched chain has fewer shapes to be in, so it pulls harder when hotter and warms when stretched, the opposite of a metal spring.
pitfall: The force in rubber is entropic, not from stretched bonds: a rubber band heated under a weight contracts, which a steel spring never does.
why: MIT OCW 3.064 Polymer Engineering lecture on chain conformation and the kinetic theory of rubber elasticity (and Feynman's much-shared rubber-band clip): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-064-polymer-engineering-fall-2003/resources/lec_6
overlapWith: carbon-polymers: that page links monomers and relates stiffness to chain length and cross-links; this one derives the restoring force from the statistics of a chain's shapes.
needsSource: none

title: Substitution mechanisms: SN1 and SN2
interaction: Step a nucleophile toward a carbon bearing a leaving group across an energy surface built from two coupled bond curves (an empirical valence-bond model) plus an ionic state whose energy drops as the solvent-polarity slider rises: the surface shows either a single pass with the nucleophile arriving from the back or a two-step route through a flat carbocation. Change the substrate from methyl to tertiary, the nucleophile's strength and concentration, and watch the computed rate law and the stereochemical outcome (clean inversion versus a racemic mix) change.
takeaway: A substitution either happens in one step from the back, inverting the molecule, or in two steps through a flat ion that either side can attack, and only the second is indifferent to how much nucleophile is present.
needs: Relative rate constants for the methyl-to-tertiary series and for solvent changes, to calibrate the model.
pitfall: The 1 and 2 count the molecules in the rate-determining step, not the number of steps, and SN1 versus SN2 is not a property of the substrate alone: solvent and nucleophile shift the balance.
why: MIT OCW 5.12 Organic Chemistry I emphasizes substitution and elimination, with a dedicated SN2/SN1 handout: https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-12-organic-chemistry-i-spring-2005/resources/sn2sn1
overlapWith: transition-state-theory (proposed): that page runs trajectories on an atom-exchange surface; this one applies the idea to the organic reaction where two competing paths explain the rate law and the stereochemistry.
needsSource: Published relative rates (the classic Hughes-Ingold and Streitwieser compilations; textbook numbers). The valence-bond parameters are fitted to these, which the page must state.

title: Catalysis on a surface
interaction: Run CO oxidation on a lattice of catalyst sites: CO lands on one empty site, O2 splits onto two neighbouring sites, and adjacent CO and O react into CO2 and leave (the Ziff-Gulari-Barshad model). Slide the CO fraction in the gas and watch the CO2 rate rise, peak and collapse as the surface smothers in CO, with the coverages plotted beside a Langmuir isotherm; raise the temperature to let CO desorb and the dead surface recover.
takeaway: A catalyst works by holding the reactants next to each other on its surface, and too much of one reactant can cover every site and stop the reaction entirely.
pitfall: A catalyst is not consumed, but it is not inert either: its activity depends on what covers it, and a poisoned surface is a catalyst that has stopped working.
why: MIT OCW 10.37 Chemical and Biological Reaction Engineering covers heterogeneous catalysis and Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-37-chemical-and-biological-reaction-engineering-spring-2007/pages/lecture-notes
overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page's catalyst only lowers a barrier; this one models the surface sites, their coverage and the poisoning that follows.
needsSource: none

title: Soap: surfactants & micelles
interaction: Drop amphiphiles, each a water-loving head on a water-fearing tail, into a box of simulated water and oil and watch them gather at the interface, then, as the reader adds more, begin forming micelles: the plot of free amphiphiles against the total shows the kink at the critical micelle concentration. Add a drop of oil and watch micelles swallow it; change the tail length and head size and see the threshold shift and the aggregates change from spheres to bilayers.
takeaway: Molecules with a water-loving head and a water-fearing tail arrange themselves to hide their tails, and above a threshold concentration they do it by forming clusters that can carry grease away.
pitfall: Soap does not break or dissolve oil molecules; it wraps them in micelles that water can carry, and the driving force is water's preference for itself, not an attraction between the tails.
why: University of Genoa soft-matter course covers the hydrophobic interaction, surface tension and self-assembly: https://corsi.unige.it/en/node/221635
overlapWith: the-cell: that page shows the membrane as a bilayer; this one models why amphiphiles assemble at all and the concentration at which they start.
needsSource: none

title: Reaction trajectories & the transition state
interaction: Fire a classical trajectory of A + BC → AB + C across a potential-energy surface (LEPS model of H + H2 and F + H2) drawn as a contour map, choosing how much energy goes into translation and how much into vibration, and see whether it crosses the saddle or turns back. Sweep the temperature to watch the Eyring rate climb, move the barrier early or late along the path to see which kind of energy gets molecules over it, and swap H for D to watch the zero-point energy and the rate change.
takeaway: A reaction is a journey over a mountain pass on an energy landscape; the pass's height sets how often molecules make it and its position sets which kind of energy gets them over.
needs: LEPS (Sato) parameters for the H3 and FH2 surfaces.
pitfall: The transition state is not an intermediate that can be isolated; it is the top of the pass, crossed in a single vibration, and a catalyst lowers the pass rather than pushing molecules over it.
why: MIT OCW 5.60 covers rates of chemical reactions and transition-state theory (Lectures 33-35): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008/resources/lec33_th
overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page draws a 1D energy profile beside colliding balls; this one computes the 2D surface and real trajectories over it, with the isotope effect as a bonus.
needsSource: Published LEPS/Sato parameters for H + H2 and F + H2 (journal numbers; no licensed dataset).

title: The critical point & supercritical fluids
interaction: Drag the temperature of a van der Waals gas (real constants for CO2 and water) and watch its isotherm on a pressure-volume plot: below a critical temperature it develops a loop that the page replaces with the flat line of the equal-area rule, which marks boiling, and the ends of all those lines trace the liquid-gas dome. Push past the critical point and the loop vanishes: compress the fluid and it goes from gas-like to liquid-like with no boiling, while a particle box beside the plot shows the meniscus disappearing.
takeaway: Above the critical temperature there is no boiling because liquid and gas have become the same phase, and a fluid there has the density of a liquid with the mobility of a gas.
needs: Critical temperature and pressure of CO2 and water.
pitfall: The loop in the van der Waals isotherm is not what a real fluid does; the flat coexistence line is, and a supercritical fluid is not a fourth state of matter.
why: MIT OCW 5.60 Thermodynamics & Kinetics (equations of state and phase equilibria lectures): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008/resources/
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page tracks a substance across its phase diagram; this one explains where the liquid-gas line ends and what lies beyond it.
needsSource: Critical constants of CO2 and water from the NIST Chemistry WebBook (free to use with citation; a handful of numbers).

title: Molecular vibrations: IR & Raman
interaction: Assemble a small molecule (HCl, CO2, H2O, CH4) from atoms and bond springs with real force constants; the page diagonalizes the Hessian and animates each normal mode. For each mode it tests whether the vibration changes the molecule's dipole or its polarizability and draws the predicted IR and Raman stick spectra next to measured line positions; swap an atom for a heavier isotope and the peaks shift.
takeaway: A molecule's IR spectrum is the set of its vibration frequencies, fixed by bond stiffness and atom masses, and a vibration appears in IR only if it moves charge and in Raman only if it changes polarizability, so CO2's symmetric stretch is silent in one and bright in the other.
needs: Harmonic force constants for the molecules (Herzberg's tabulations) and measured band positions for comparison.
pitfall: CO2 is a greenhouse gas because its bend and asymmetric stretch change its dipole, not because it is a gas that traps heat; N2 and O2 vibrate too but stay invisible in IR.
why: MIT OCW 5.61 covers molecular spectroscopy, and OCR/AQA A-level chemistry assess IR spectra with an absorption data sheet: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/
overlapWith: greenhouse-effect: that page takes absorption as an input; this one computes which vibrations absorb and why from the molecule's own mechanics.
needsSource: HITRAN line lists for CO2, H2O, HCl and CH4 (free with citation per hitran.org; the 1986 edition mirror at NCAR is CC BY 4.0). NIST WebBook IR spectra are free to view but their redistribution terms are not clearly open, so the page should rely on HITRAN.

title: X-ray diffraction: reading a crystal
interaction: Pick a real crystal structure (NaCl, CsCl, diamond, copper, silicon) and the page computes its structure factors and draws the powder pattern against angle from Bragg's law and the atomic scattering factors; rotate a single crystal to see the spots of its reciprocal lattice pass through the Ewald sphere. Edit the cell by swapping an atom, deleting one or changing the lattice type, and watch peaks appear, vanish or shift; change the X-ray wavelength and the whole pattern rescales.
takeaway: A diffraction pattern is the crystal's Fourier transform: peak positions come from the spacing of the lattice and peak intensities from where the atoms sit in the cell, so the missing peaks are as telling as the present ones.
needs: CIF files for the structures and atomic scattering-factor coefficients.
pitfall: Bragg 'reflection' is not a mirror bouncing a beam off a plane: every atom scatters in all directions and the peaks are where those waves add up, which is why intensities depend on the atoms and not only on the planes.
why: MIT OCW 3.091 Fall 2018 runs through crystallography and x-rays: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-091-introduction-to-solid-state-chemistry-fall-2018/pages/syllabus/
overlapWith: semiconductors: that page shows lattices beside their bands; this one computes what X-rays see in a lattice and how structures are solved from it.
needsSource: Crystallography Open Database entries (COD states they are free to download, reuse and redistribute; confirm its public-domain statement on crystallography.net); scattering factors from the Waasmaier-Kirfel or Cromer-Mann parameterisations as redistributed in BSD-licensed xraylib (the International Tables themselves are copyrighted).
